notes.front: What is a qualified tuition program (QTP)?
notes.back: A qualified tuition program (QTP), or 529 plan: a state or school programme for prepaying or saving towards a student’s qualified education expenses.
notes.explanation: States may run either a prepaid or a savings version; eligible educational institutions may run prepaid ones. Pub 970 notes that QTPs are also called 529 plans.
notes.example: Like a savings account earmarked for one student’s college costs, but set up under a state’s or a college’s programme.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Qualified Tuition Program (QTP)”, p. 49
notes.evidence: QTPs are also called 529 plans. States may establish and maintain programs that allow you to either prepay or contribute to an account for paying a student’s qualified education expenses at an eligible educational institution.

notes.front: What is a Coverdell education savings account (Coverdell ESA)?
notes.back: A trust or custodial account created in the United States only to pay one beneficiary’s qualified education expenses; also called a Coverdell ESA.
notes.explanation: Pub 970 defines it as a trust or custodial account created in the United States only for that purpose, and it must be designated a Coverdell ESA when it is created.
notes.example: Like a savings account opened for one child’s school costs, but set up as a trust and labelled a Coverdell ESA from day one.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “What Is a Coverdell ESA?”, p. 38
notes.evidence: A Coverdell ESA is a trust or custodial account created or organized in the United States only for the purpose of paying the qualified education expenses of the Designated beneficiary

notes.front: What is community property, and when does it change a federal return?
notes.back: A state-law system of marital property and income; it changes the federal return of a married person in a community property state who files separately.
notes.explanation: Separate filers must work out their community income and their separate income. Pub 555 lists nine community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin.
notes.example: Like a partnership in which each partner owns half the profits, but created by the marriage laws of a state such as California.
notes.source: Publication 555 (Rev. December 2024), Community Property, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Community property laws affect how you figure your income on your federal income tax return if you are married, live in a community property state or country, and file separate returns.

notes.front: Who is an injured spouse?
notes.back: A spouse on a joint return whose joint overpayment was (or will be) applied to the other spouse’s past-due obligation; they file Form 8379.
notes.explanation: The offset takes a refund that is partly theirs to pay a debt that is only the other spouse’s; Form 8379 is how they ask for their share back.
notes.example: Like a joint bank account frozen to pay one holder’s old debt, when the other holder’s money was in it too.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8379 (Rev. November 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Form 8379 is filed by one spouse (the injured spouse) on a jointly filed tax return when the joint overpayment was (or is expected to be) applied (offset) to a past-due obligation of the other spouse.

notes.front: What is innocent spouse relief?
notes.back: Relief from tax, interest and penalties on a joint return when the spouse (or former spouse) improperly reported or omitted items.
notes.explanation: Generally the tax, interest and penalties that qualify for relief can then be collected only from the other spouse (or former spouse).
notes.example: Like a co-signer being released from a loan because the other borrower hid facts from them, but for tax on a joint return.
notes.source: Publication 971 (Rev. December 2021), Innocent Spouse Relief, “Innocent Spouse Relief”, p. 5
notes.evidence: By requesting innocent spouse relief, you can be relieved of responsibility for paying tax, interest, and penalties if your spouse (or former spouse) improperly reported items or omitted items on your tax return.

notes.front: What does joint and several liability mean for a joint return?
notes.back: Both spouses are generally liable for the tax, and the entire liability may be assessed against either one.
notes.explanation: Pub 17 gives this as the consequence of filing a joint return, which both spouses must sign even if only one had income.
notes.example: Like two people who co-sign a loan: the lender can ask either of them for the full balance.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Signatures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: entire tax liability may be assessed against either spouse. See chapter 2.

notes.front: What is a claim for refund, for an individual?
notes.back: A request, usually on Form 1040-X (the amended return), to correct a filed return and get back tax overpaid.
notes.explanation: Pub 17 says that if you discover an error you can file an amended return or claim for refund; the Form 1040-X instructions set the time limits for a credit or refund.
notes.example: Like returning to a shop with the receipt after being overcharged, but with a deadline and a form.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Amended Returns and Claims for Refund”, p. 20
notes.evidence: If you discover an error, you can file an amended return or claim for refund.

notes.front: How much income do you report from bartering, and when?
notes.back: The fair market value of the property or services you receive, included at the time you receive them.
notes.explanation: Bartering is an exchange of property or services, so no cash changes hands; Pub 525 says the income is generally reported on Schedule C (Form 1040).
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Bartering”, p. 20
notes.evidence: You must include in your income, at the time received, the FMV of property or services you receive in bartering.

notes.front: Farah, a self-employed web designer, builds a website for a bakery in 2025. Instead of cash she receives catering worth $1,200. What must she report?
notes.back: $1,200 of income: the fair market value of the catering she received, generally on Schedule C (Form 1040).
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because no cash changed hands
B) $1,200 of income, generally on Schedule C
C) Income only if the bakery sends her a Form 1099
notes.choicesExplained: A: bartering income is the fair market value of what you receive, not cash. C: the rule to include it does not depend on receiving a form.
notes.explanation: She exchanged services for property, which is bartering, so she includes the value received when she receives it: $1,200.
notes.source: Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, “Bartering”, p. 20
notes.evidence: Generally, you report this income on Schedule C (Form 1040).

notes.front: What is the maximum capital gain rate on collectibles gain, such as from an antique or a coin held more than 1 year?
notes.explanation: Pub 550 defines collectibles gain as gain from selling items such as art, rugs, antiques, bullion, gems, stamps, coins or alcoholic beverages held more than 1 year, and Table 4-4 caps it at 28%.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Gain Tax Rates”, p. 103
notes.evidence: This is gain or loss from the sale or trade of a work of art, rug, antique, metal (such as gold, silver, and platinum bullion), gem, stamp, coin, or alcoholic beverage held more than 1 year.

notes.front: For federal tax, payments or contributions to a qualified tuition program (QTP) are {{c1::not deductible}}.
notes.back: Not deductible.
notes.explanation: Pub 970 says plainly that you can’t deduct either payments or contributions to a QTP.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Qualified Tuition Program (QTP)”, p. 49
notes.evidence: You can’t deduct either payments or contributions to a QTP.

notes.front: Ines puts $4,000 into her state’s 529 plan for her grandson in 2025 and asks you to deduct it on her federal Form 1040. What do you tell her?
notes.back: She cannot: contributions to a QTP are not deductible on the federal return.
notes.choices:
A) Deduct the full $4,000 as an itemized deduction
B) No federal deduction for the contribution
C) Deduct it only if her grandson is her dependent
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: Pub 970 allows no deduction for payments or contributions to a QTP, whoever the beneficiary is.
notes.explanation: Pub 970 says QTPs are also called 529 plans, so her state plan is a QTP, and the rule allowing no deduction applies whoever the beneficiary is.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Qualified Tuition Program (QTP)”, p. 49
notes.evidence: QTPs are also called 529 plans.

notes.front: What is the annual contribution limit for Coverdell ESAs, and is it per account or per beneficiary?
notes.back: $2,000 per designated beneficiary, however many Coverdell ESAs are set up for that beneficiary.
notes.explanation: Pub 970 sets the limit for each beneficiary, no matter how many accounts exist or how many individuals contribute.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Coverdell ESA, contributions”, p. 40
notes.evidence: The annual contribution limit is $2,000 for each beneficiary, no matter how many Coverdell ESAs are set up for that beneficiary.

notes.front: In 2025 two grandparents each want to put $1,500 into separate Coverdell ESAs for the same 10-year-old grandson. Can both contributions be made in full?
notes.back: No. Together they would be $3,000, and the limit is $2,000 per beneficiary however many people contribute.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: each contributor has a separate $2,000 limit
B) Yes: each account has a separate $2,000 limit
C) No: the combined $3,000 is over the $2,000 limit per beneficiary
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the $2,000 limit applies to the beneficiary, no matter how many individuals contribute or how many accounts exist.
notes.explanation: $1,500 + $1,500 = $3,000, which is $1,000 over the $2,000 limit for one beneficiary.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “Coverdell ESA, contributions”, p. 40
notes.evidence: The annual contribution limit is $2,000 per beneficiary, no matter how many individuals contribute.

notes.front: A parent wants to open a new Coverdell ESA for her 19-year-old son, who is not a special needs beneficiary. Can she?
notes.back: No. When a Coverdell ESA is established, the beneficiary must be under 18 or a special needs beneficiary.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any student can be a beneficiary
B) No, he is over the age limit for a new account
C) Yes, if she contributes no more than $2,000
notes.choicesExplained: A: the age rule applies when the account is established. C: the contribution limit does not cure the age rule.
notes.explanation: At 19 and without special needs, he fails the under-18 condition that applies when the account is set up.
notes.source: Publication 970 (2025), Tax Benefits for Education, “What Is a Coverdell ESA?”, p. 38
notes.evidence: When the account is established, the designated beneficiary must be under age 18 or a special needs beneficiary.

notes.front: What is generally the basis of property inherited from a decedent?
notes.back: Its fair market value at the date of death (or on the alternate valuation date, if the estate elects it).
notes.explanation: Pub 551 lists these as the general choices; where Form 8971 reports an estate tax value, certain beneficiaries must use that value as their initial basis.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Inherited Property”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Generally, the basis of property inherited from a decedent is one of the following. 1. The FMV of the property at the date of the individual's death.

notes.front: You receive a gift whose fair market value is at least the donor’s adjusted basis. What is your basis?
notes.back: The donor’s adjusted basis at the time of the gift, increased by all or part of any gift tax paid.
notes.explanation: The donor’s basis carries over to you rather than being reset to market value; the gift tax adjustment depends on the date of the gift.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Property Received as a Gift”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If the FMV of the property is equal to or greater than the donor's adjusted basis, your basis is the donor's adjusted basis at the time you received the gift.

notes.front: You gave appreciated shares to your father, who died 8 months later and left them back to you. Do you get a date-of-death value basis?
notes.back: No. Your basis is your father’s adjusted basis immediately before his death, not the fair market value.
notes.explanation: The date-of-death rule does not apply to appreciated property you or your spouse gave the decedent within 1 year before the death.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Inherited Property: Appreciated property”, p. 15
notes.evidence: The above rule doesn't apply to appreciated property you receive from a decedent if you or your spouse originally gave the property to the decedent within 1 year before the decedent's death.

notes.front: Rosa bought shares for $20,000; they are now worth $80,000. She gives them to her son, who sells them at once for $80,000. What is his gain?
notes.back: $60,000: his basis is Rosa’s $20,000 adjusted basis (ignoring any gift tax), because the value was above her basis.
notes.choices:
A) $0, because his basis is the $80,000 value
B) $60,000, because Rosa’s $20,000 basis carries over
C) $80,000, because a gift has no basis
notes.choicesExplained: A: a stepped-up value applies to inherited property, not to a gift like this. C: a gift carries the donor’s adjusted basis.
notes.explanation: Value ($80,000) is at least Rosa’s basis ($20,000), so his basis is $20,000. Gain = $80,000 − $20,000 = $60,000. Had he inherited them at an $80,000 date-of-death value, the gain would have been $0.
notes.source: Publication 551 (Rev. December 2025), Basis of Assets, “Property Received as a Gift”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If the FMV of the property is equal to or greater than the donor's adjusted basis, your basis is the donor's adjusted basis at the time you received the gift.

notes.front: How is a withdrawal (not taken as an annuity) from an annuity contract taxed if made on or after the annuity starting date?
notes.back: The entire amount withdrawn is generally taxable.
notes.explanation: Pub 575 contrasts this with withdrawals before the annuity starting date, where part may be tax free depending on the plan.
notes.source: Publication 575 (2025), Pension and Annuity Income, “Withdrawals”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If you withdraw funds (other than as an annuity) on or after your annuity starting date, the entire amount withdrawn is generally taxable.

notes.front: Lena is married, domiciled in Texas and files separately. Rent comes in from a house she owns as separate property. Is the rent community or separate income?
notes.back: Community income: Texas treats income from separate property as community income.
notes.choices:
A) Separate income, because the house is separate property
B) Community income, under Texas law
C) Neither: rent is outside community property rules
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the rule in Arizona, California, Nevada, New Mexico and Washington, not Texas. C: separate filers must sort all income into community and separate.
notes.explanation: Community property states differ on income from separate property; Pub 555 puts Texas with Idaho, Louisiana and Wisconsin, which treat it as community income.
notes.source: Publication 555 (Rev. December 2024), Community Property, “Income from separate property”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Other states characterize income from separate property as community income. These states include Idaho, Louisiana, Texas, and Wisconsin.

notes.front: Is gain or loss generally recognized when property passes between spouses, or former spouses because of a divorce?
notes.back: No. Generally no gain or loss is recognized, though a gift tax return may be needed.
notes.explanation: Pub 504 applies the rule even when the transfer is in exchange for cash, release of marital rights or assumption of liabilities.
notes.source: Publication 504 (2025), Divorced or Separated Individuals, “Property Settlements”, p. 18
notes.evidence: Generally, there is no recognized gain or loss on the transfer of property between spouses, or between former spouses, if the transfer is because of a divorce.

notes.front: How is alimony treated under a divorce or separation instrument executed after 2018?
notes.back: Not deductible by the payer and not included in the recipient’s income.
notes.explanation: The same applies to a pre-2019 instrument modified after 2018 if the modification expressly says so.
notes.source: Publication 504 (2025), Divorced or Separated Individuals, “Alimony”, p. 16
notes.evidence: alimony or separate maintenance payments under a divorce or separation instrument executed after 2018 won't be deductible by the payer. Such amounts also won't be includible in the income of the recipient.

notes.front: As part of their divorce, Sam transfers to Ria a rental condo with an adjusted basis of $150,000 and a value of $400,000. What is Ria’s basis?
notes.back: $150,000, Sam’s adjusted basis; Sam recognizes no gain on the transfer.
notes.choices:
A) $400,000, its value at the transfer
B) $150,000, Sam’s adjusted basis
C) $275,000, the average of the two
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: property received from a spouse or, incident to divorce, a former spouse keeps the transferor’s adjusted basis, whatever its value.
notes.explanation: Her basis is his $150,000 adjusted basis, and it applies to both gain and loss when she later sells. The $250,000 of built-in gain ($400,000 − $150,000) moves to her.
notes.source: Publication 504 (2025), Divorced or Separated Individuals, “Basis of property received”, p. 19
notes.evidence: Your basis in property received from your spouse (or former spouse, if incident to your divorce) is the same as your spouse's adjusted basis. This applies for determining either gain or loss when you later dispose of the property.

notes.front: How much net capital loss can an individual deduct against other income in a year?
notes.back: Up to $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately); a larger loss becomes a capital loss carryover.
notes.explanation: The limit is figured on Schedule D (Form 1040), so the part over the limit affects future returns rather than this one.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Losses”, p. 101
notes.evidence: $3,000 ($1,500 if you are married and file a separate return), or • Your total net loss as shown on line 16 of Schedule D (Form 1040). You can use your total net loss to reduce your income dollar for dollar, up to the $3,000 limit. Capital loss carryover.

notes.front: Which form claims the prior year minimum tax credit?
notes.back: Form 8801.
notes.explanation: Pub 17 lists the prior year minimum tax credit among the credits and points to Form 8801, so an alternative minimum tax item from an earlier year can reach a later return.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Other credits”, p. 109
notes.evidence: Prior year minimum tax credit. See Form 8801.

notes.front: Do the usual refund time limits necessarily apply to a claim based on a net operating loss carryback?
notes.back: Not necessarily. It is a special type of refund; the rules are in Form 172 and its instructions.
notes.explanation: Pub 17 says the usual dates and limits may not apply to the items on its list, which includes net operating loss carrybacks.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Exceptions for special types of refunds”, p. 21
notes.evidence: the dates and limits discussed earlier may not apply. These items, and where to get more information, are as follows. • Bad debt. See Pub. 550. • Worthless security. See Pub. 550. • Foreign tax paid or accrued. See Pub. 514. • Net operating loss carryback. See Form 172 and the Instructions for Form 172.

notes.front: What happens to a qualified business net loss for the year on Form 8995?
notes.back: It is carried forward to next year; generally no qualified business income deduction is allowed this year.
notes.explanation: The instructions allow the deduction in a loss year only if there is certain other qualifying income, such as qualified income from a publicly traded partnership.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8995 (2025), “Line 4”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If you have a qualified business net loss for the year, you don't qualify for the QBI deduction unless you have qualified REIT dividends or qualified PTP income. The loss will be carried forward to next year.

notes.front: Ana, single, has a total net capital loss of $7,500 on Schedule D for 2025. How much can she deduct in 2025, and how much carries over?
notes.back: Deduct $3,000 in 2025; carry over $4,500.
notes.choices:
A) Deduct $7,500 in 2025
B) Deduct $3,000; carry over $4,500
C) Deduct $1,500; carry over $6,000
notes.choicesExplained: A: the deduction is capped at $3,000. C: $1,500 is the cap only for married filing separately.
notes.explanation: Her deduction is the lesser of $3,000 or her $7,500 net loss, so $3,000. $7,500 − $3,000 = $4,500 carried over.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Losses”, p. 101
notes.evidence: You can use your total net loss to reduce your income dollar for dollar, up to the $3,000 limit.

notes.front: What may an injured spouse get back by filing Form 8379?
notes.back: Their share of the joint refund.
notes.explanation: The refund was offset against the other spouse’s past-due obligation; Form 8379 lets the injured spouse ask for the part that was theirs.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8379 (Rev. November 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: By filing Form 8379, the injured spouse may be able to get back their share of the joint refund.

notes.front: Which type of relief from joint liability allocates the understated tax on a joint return between the spouses?
notes.back: Separation of liability relief; each spouse is generally responsible for the part allocated to them.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three types of relief for joint filers; Pub 971 notes it gives no refund for liabilities already paid.
notes.source: Publication 971 (Rev. December 2021), Innocent Spouse Relief, “Separation of Liability Relief”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Under this type of relief, the understated tax (plus interest and penalties) on your joint return is allocated between you and your spouse (or former spouse).

notes.front: Which type of relief from joint liability can be considered only if you are not eligible for innocent spouse relief or separation of liability relief?
notes.back: Equitable relief.
notes.explanation: Being ineligible for the other two types is one of equitable relief’s threshold conditions, along with having filed a joint return.
notes.source: Publication 971 (Rev. December 2021), Innocent Spouse Relief, “Equitable Relief”, p. 8
notes.evidence: 1. You are not eligible for innocent spouse relief or separation of liability relief. 2. You filed a joint return for the tax year(s) at issue.

notes.front: Injured spouse or innocent spouse relief: which form is each, and what does each fix?
notes.back: Injured spouse: Form 8379, recovers your refund share taken for your spouse’s debt. Innocent spouse relief: Form 8857, relieves tax caused by your spouse’s items.
notes.explanation: The Form 8379 instructions tell you not to use Form 8379 to claim innocent spouse relief, and to file Form 8857 instead.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8379 (Rev. November 2024), “Innocent Spouse Relief”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Don't file Form 8379 if you are claiming innocent spouse relief. Instead, file Form 8857.

notes.front: Priya and Tom file jointly. Their whole refund is applied to Tom’s past-due obligation from before they married; Priya had wages and withholding. What should Priya file?
notes.back: Form 8379, as the injured spouse, to try to get back her share of the joint refund.
notes.choices:
A) Form 8857, for innocent spouse relief
B) Form 8379, as the injured spouse
C) Nothing: joint refunds cannot be split
notes.choicesExplained: A: innocent spouse relief is for tax due to a spouse’s wrongly reported items, not a refund offset. C: Form 8379 exists to recover the injured spouse’s share.
notes.explanation: The joint overpayment was offset against the other spouse’s past-due obligation, which is exactly the Form 8379 situation.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 8379 (Rev. November 2024), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: By filing Form 8379, the injured spouse may be able to get back their share of the joint refund.

notes.front: Mei signed a joint return. Her husband left off consulting income she did not know, and had no reason to know, about. The IRS assesses more tax. What relief fits?
notes.back: Innocent spouse relief, requested on Form 8857, if all its conditions are met, including unfairness.
notes.choices:
A) Injured spouse allocation on Form 8379
B) Innocent spouse relief on Form 8857
C) None: joint filers can never be relieved
notes.choicesExplained: A: Form 8379 recovers a refund share taken for a spouse’s debt, not an understated tax. C: Pub 971 offers three types of relief to joint filers.
notes.explanation: The understated tax comes from her spouse’s erroneous item, and she lacked knowledge and reason to know; she must also show it would be unfair to hold her liable.
notes.source: Publication 971 (Rev. December 2021), Innocent Spouse Relief, “Innocent Spouse Relief”, p. 5
notes.evidence: You can show that when you signed the joint return you did not know, and had no reason to know, that the understated tax existed (or the extent to which the understated tax existed).

notes.front: Under the general rule, what total must you pay through withholding and estimated tax for 2025 to avoid the penalty?
notes.back: The smaller of 90% of your expected 2025 tax or 100% of the tax shown on your 2024 return.
notes.explanation: The 2024 return must cover all 12 months; different percentages apply to farmers and fishers and to certain higher income taxpayers.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Required Annual Payment: General rule”, p. 22
notes.evidence: General rule. The total amount you must pay is the smaller of: 1. 90% of your total expected tax for 2025, or 2. 100% of the total tax shown on your 2024 return.

notes.front: When does the prior-year part of the estimated tax rule rise from 100% to 110%?
notes.back: When 2024 AGI was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately for 2025).
notes.explanation: Pub 505 substitutes 110% for 100% of the prior-year tax for these higher income taxpayers, unless the farming or fishing rule applies.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Higher Income Taxpayers”, p. 21
notes.evidence: If your AGI for 2024 was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if your filing status for 2025 is married filing a separate return), substitute 110% for 100% in (2b) under General Rule, earlier.

notes.front: Omar, single, had 2024 AGI of $180,000 and 2024 tax of $30,000. He expects 2025 tax of $40,000. What total payment avoids the penalty?
notes.back: $33,000: 110% of his 2024 tax, which is smaller than 90% of his expected 2025 tax ($36,000).
notes.choicesExplained: A: his 2024 AGI was over $150,000, so 110% replaces 100%. C: the required payment is the smaller of the two figures, and $33,000 is smaller.
notes.explanation: Because his 2024 AGI exceeded $150,000, the prior-year figure uses 110%: 110% × $30,000 = $33,000. The current-year figure is 90% × $40,000 = $36,000; the required payment is the lower one.
notes.source: Publication 505 (2025), Tax Withholding and Estimated Tax, “Higher Income Taxpayers”, p. 21
notes.evidence: If your AGI for 2024 was more than $150,000 ($75,000 if your filing status for 2025 is married filing a separate return), substitute 110% for 100% in (2b) under General Rule, earlier.

notes.front: Under the cash method, in which year is income reported and in which year are expenses generally deducted?
notes.back: Income in the year actually or constructively received; expenses generally in the year actually paid.
notes.explanation: Pub 17 says this is the method most individual taxpayers use, so for them the year of payment generally sets the year of a deduction.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Accounting Methods: Cash method”, p. 14
notes.evidence: If you use this method, report all items of income in the year in which you actually or constructively receive them. Generally, you deduct all expenses in the year you actually pay them.

notes.front: What character of gain or loss generally results from selling a capital asset, and from selling a noncapital asset?
notes.back: Capital asset: capital gain or loss. Noncapital asset: generally ordinary gain or loss.
notes.explanation: Property used in a trade or business may be treated either way, as Pub 544 explains.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital or Ordinary Gain or Loss”, p. 75
notes.evidence: Generally, a sale or trade of a capital asset (defined next) results in a capital gain or loss. A sale or trade of a noncapital asset generally results in ordinary gain or loss.

notes.front: Jo sells, at a gain, shares she held in her personal brokerage account as an investment. Is it a capital or an ordinary gain?
notes.back: A capital gain: stocks held in a personal account are capital assets.
notes.choices:
A) Capital gain
B) Ordinary gain
C) Neither: gains on personal investments are not taxed
notes.choicesExplained: B: ordinary gain generally comes from noncapital assets. C: the gain on a capital asset is a taxable capital gain.
notes.explanation: Pub 550 counts almost everything owned for personal use, pleasure or investment as a capital asset, and names stocks in a personal account as an example.
notes.source: Publication 550 (2025), Investment Income and Expenses, “Capital Assets and Noncapital Assets”, p. 75
notes.evidence: For the most part, everything you own and use for personal purposes, pleasure, or investment is a capital asset. Some examples are: • Stocks or bonds held in your personal account;

notes.front: Does a divorce decree making the former spouse solely responsible for a joint-return tax stop the IRS collecting from you?
notes.back: No. You remain jointly and severally liable, and the IRS can still collect from you.
notes.explanation: Pub 971 says the liability survives a later divorce whatever the decree says; relief comes only through its three types of relief.
notes.source: Publication 971 (Rev. December 2021), Innocent Spouse Relief, “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: You remain jointly and severally liable for taxes, and the IRS can still collect them from you, even if you later divorce and the divorce decree states that your former spouse will be solely responsible for the tax.

notes.front: Ben and Ava filed a joint 2024 return that shows $6,000 of unpaid tax. Only Ben had income. Can the IRS assess the whole $6,000 against Ava?
notes.back: Yes. On a joint return both spouses are generally liable, and the entire liability may be assessed against either.
notes.choices:
A) No, only against Ben, who earned the income
B) Only half, $3,000, against each
C) Yes, the entire $6,000 against either spouse
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: joint and several liability does not depend on who earned the income or split it in halves.
notes.explanation: Both had to sign the joint return even though only Ben had income, and that joint filing makes the whole tax collectible from either.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Signatures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: If you file a joint return, both you and your spouse must sign the return, even if only one of you had income.

notes.front: By when must Form 1040-X be filed to claim a credit or refund?
notes.back: Within 3 years (including extensions) after filing the original return, or 2 years after paying the tax, whichever is later.
notes.explanation: The time limit can be suspended for people physically or mentally unable to manage their financial affairs.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040-X (Rev. December 2025), “When To File”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Generally, for a credit or refund, you must file Form 1040-X within 3 years (including extensions) after the date you filed your original return or within 2 years after the date you paid the tax, whichever is later.

notes.front: For the refund time limit, when is a return filed early (say, on 1 March) treated as filed?
notes.back: On the due date, generally April 15.
notes.explanation: A return filed during an extension period, by contrast, counts as filed on the day it was received.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040-X (Rev. December 2025), “When To File”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you filed your original return early (for example, March 1 for a calendar year return), your return is considered filed on the due date (generally April 15).

notes.front: Kofi filed his 2025 return on 10 February 2026 and paid all tax by then; the due date is 15 April 2026. By when must he file Form 1040-X for a refund?
notes.back: By 15 April 2029: 3 years from the due date, when his early return is treated as filed.
notes.choices:
A) 10 February 2029
B) 15 April 2029
C) 15 April 2028
notes.choicesExplained: A: an early return counts as filed on the due date, not the day it was sent. C: that is only 2 years after payment, and the later deadline applies.
notes.explanation: Deemed filing date 15 April 2026 + 3 years = 15 April 2029. The 2-year-from-payment limit would end earlier, and the later of the two applies.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040-X (Rev. December 2025), “When To File”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you filed your original return early (for example, March 1 for a calendar year return), your return is considered filed on the due date (generally April 15).

notes.front: If someone else prepares your Form 1040, who is responsible for the correctness of the return?
notes.back: You are, and you must still sign and date the return.
notes.explanation: The Form 1040 instructions say that having someone prepare your return does not shift responsibility for its correctness.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Sign Your Return”, p. 65
notes.evidence: Be sure to date your return and enter your occupation(s). If you have someone prepare your return, you are still responsible for the correctness of the return.
